option: s&box (Facepunch, Source 2 + C#/.NET 10) — sbox.game, Steam app 590830
oneLine: The "easy publishing" premise is backwards — s&box's own platform has ~695 concurrent players behind a $20 paywall and its standalone-Steam export is still an approval-gated preview, so choosing it would mean a 100% rewrite of an explicitly web-native spec in exchange for a smaller audience, a harder publishing path, and more IP-takedown exposure, not less.
strengths: Language/runtime is genuinely excellent for this workload: C# on .NET 10, with structs, Span<T>, array-of-struct layouts and manual pooling. A 2,000-entity fixed-timestep sim with zero steady-state allocation is materially EASIER to hit in C# than in JS — you get real value types and deterministic memory layout instead of fighting hidden classes and the JS GC.

Code is plain text files. Gameplay C# lives in a `code/` folder at project root, with a modern `.slnx` solution openable in VS 2022/2026, VS Code, Cursor, or Rider. Nothing forces you into a proprietary visual scripting tool for the simulation layer — an AI agent CAN author the game logic as ordinary .cs files.

Hot reload is best-in-class: save a .cs or .razor file and the editor recompiles and swaps it in while you are still in Play mode. For a tuning-heavy genre where you iterate on damage numbers 200 times a day, that is a real advantage over a browser refresh.

2D is no longer a hack. A `Sprite` resource and `SpriteRenderer` component are now in-engine (the old Facepunch `sbox-spritetools` library is explicitly marked OBSOLETE because it was absorbed), `CameraComponent` supports true orthographic projection with an `OrthographicSize` parameter, pixel-art texture filtering modes are exposed, and a tileset editor landed around the July 2026 update.
Existence proof for the exact genre: a top-down Vampire-Survivors-like 2D roguelite has already been built and shipped on the s&box platform. This is not theoretical.

Zero royalties and zero revenue share, and the engine layer was open-sourced under MIT in November 2025 — so an agent (and you) can read the actual engine source when the docs are thin, which partially offsets the documentation gap.
Standalone export, when it opens up, carries no engine royalty at all — better commercial terms than Unity's historical stance and comparable to Godot.
Headless execution genuinely exists (dedicated servers run without rendering), so a simulation harness is not architecturally impossible.
dealbreakers: THE PUBLISHING CLAIM IS FALSE — this is the single most important finding. s&box's own platform audience is ~695 concurrent players as of today (25 Jul 2026), down from a 6,762 all-time peak on release day (28 Apr 2026); the June 2026 average was 748, versus 4,106 in April — a 59.5% month-over-month collapse and roughly 90% off peak. That is the TOTAL platform, split across every game on it, and every one of those players had to pay $19.99 to get in. Shipping there is not 'easy publishing', it is publishing to a nearly empty room behind a paywall.

Standalone export — the thing that would actually let you sell on Steam — is STILL IN PREVIEW and gated. Facepunch signed the Valve license in late March 2026, but the docs (last updated ~26 Apr 2026) still say distribution requires approval from Valve, that it is being piloted with a few selected developers first (My Summer Cottage as the pilot), and that you must NOT distribute exported builds without a license, directing you to email standalone@facepunch.com. Garry's own framing: 'We still have work to do on our end. We need to create a license between Facepunch and the people shipping games, then double and triple check everything is legit.' You would be betting a multi-month solo project on a discretionary approval queue that did not exist a few months ago and has no published SLA.

The standalone license reportedly requires that the game be on Steam if it is on any storefront at all. That contractually kills the cheapest, fastest, lowest-risk distribution path for this exact game — an itch.io release. You cannot do itch-first, itch-only, or a free browser demo to build an audience.

NO WEB EXPORT, and the spec is a web game. s&box is PC-only: no browser/WebAssembly target, no console, no mobile. The spec mandates 'Opens from index.html with no build step and no network requests', localStorage persistence, a `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` URL parameter for the harness, and touch controls with a virtual stick. Every one of those is a hard acceptance criterion in Section 17, and s&box breaks all of them outright.
Touch support is impossible. Section 17 requires 'Keyboard, mouse, gamepad, and touch all fully playable.' s&box has no mobile target. That criterion cannot be met, period.

Hardware target conflict: s&box's minimum spec is Windows 10 64-bit, i5-7500/Ryzen 5 1600, 8GB RAM, GTX 1050/RX 470 — and Intel integrated graphics are explicitly NOT SUPPORTED (only AMD APUs work). The spec's target is '60 FPS on a mid-range laptop'. An enormous share of mid-range laptops are Intel iGPU machines. The Canvas 2D build runs on all of them, plus Chromebooks and phones. The s&box build refuses to launch.

The AI-coding-agent premise — which is the whole delivery plan here — is actively undermined. A March 2026 analysis lays out why: models' training data predates the November 2025 open-source release; 's&box C# isn't Unity C#... The component lifecycle, the networking model, the scene system... none of it maps'; 's&box runs a restricted .NET subset' so agents confidently emit blocked APIs like System.IO.File; and 'the total volume of s&box-specific code and documentation available on the open internet is a fraction of what exists for established engines', which drives hallucination. Vanilla JS + Canvas 2D is arguably the single best-represented target in any coding model's training set. You would be trading the agent's strongest domain for one of its weakest.

Violent breaking-change history on a project that must survive months of solo work. In August 2023 Facepunch deleted the entire client/server Entity system and replaced it with a Unity-style Scene/Component model. Garry's own words: 'the time will come when no client/server games work anymore, which means that most of the games people have created in s&box thus far are unplayable. And that sucks. And I'm sorry.' That is not ancient history in effect — the community VS-like referenced above was 'originally made in the Entity system but later re-created using the 2D Sprite Tools', i.e. someone paid that rewrite tax on this exact genre. Facepunch's own docs warned that 'breaking changes happen often and the API is not yet complete.' 1.0 shipped Apr 2026, which reduces but does not eliminate this risk.

The sandbox accesslist forces an either/or you cannot straddle. Platform games are scanned post-compile and refuse to load if they touch anything outside the whitelist — no System.IO.File, no Process.Start, no DllImport, no reflection. Standalone builds can disable the whitelist for full .NET, but doing so makes the project unpublishable to the s&box platform. So you cannot ship one build that both lives on the platform and has the file/process access a 100x offline balance harness wants.

IP EXPOSURE IS WORSE ON A THIRD-PARTY PLATFORM, NOT BETTER — and this spec is 19 characters that are each explicitly 1:1 on Gawr Gura, Mori Calliope, Houshou Marine, Kiryu Coco, Kizuna AI, Goku, Gohan, Naruto, Sasuke, Light Yagami, Tanjiro, and Mikoto Misaka, on stages that are Wall Maria, the Hidden Leaf Village, and the Infinity Castle. The s&box EULA requires you not 'infringe any third party rights', grants Facepunch a 'non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, sub-licensable, assignable licence' over your Experiences, and reserves the right to 'temporarily or permanently suspend or cancel your access to s&box without prior warning' and remove Experiences with no refunds. Monetization rules separately forbid monetizing packages built on copyrighted material. Facepunch runs a public DMCA reporting endpoint. Net effect: Cover Corp or Shueisha files one complaint, and a company with its own Valve relationship to protect deletes you instantly, with no counter-notice process and no obligation to hear you out. Self-publishing keeps you inside the DMCA safe-harbor framework, where you get a formal counter-notice with legal weight, you keep control of your own binary, and itch.io is famously hands-off. The spec's own mitigation — the DEV_MODE ref-name stripping and the one-to-one rule — is designed for self-publishing and does nothing against a nervous platform moderator.

Revenue on-platform is discretionary charity, not sales. There is no direct game-sales mechanism for creators on s&box; you get The Play Fund, which the EULA says creators 'do not have any right to compensation' from and which Facepunch 'operates at its sole and absolute discretion' and can 'suspend or discontinue at any time'. It was doubled to $1M after launch backlash — split across the whole creator base.

Discovery on-platform is hostile to exactly this project. s&box launched to 'Mixed' Steam reviews (~44%) with the front page overrun by AI-generated content; Garry publicly committed to 'push obviously AI-created slop off the main page.' A game built by an AI coding agent whose shipping art direction is emoji and procedurally drawn shapes is going to be pattern-matched as precisely that — by both the discovery algorithm and by users — regardless of how good the underlying 2,000-entity simulation is.
Windows-only editor. No Mac or Linux development, and no Mac/Linux/Steam Deck build target for players.

facts.claim: s&box left beta and released on Steam on 28 April 2026 at $19.99 as a full (non-Early-Access) release, after a free public preview that opened in July 2024.

s&box's all-time concurrent peak was 6,762 players on 28 Apr 2026 (release day). As of 25 July 2026 it sits at ~695 concurrent. Monthly averages: April 2026 = 4,106, June 2026 = 748 — a 59.54% decline, roughly 90% below peak.

s&box launched to 'Mixed' Steam reviews (~44% positive) with the front page dominated by AI-generated content; it still grossed ~$1M on launch day. Garry Newman responded that Facepunch would 'push obviously AI-created slop off the main page' while continuing to permit AI-assisted creation, and doubled the Play Fund to $1M.

In late March 2026 Facepunch signed a license with Valve permitting royalty-free standalone Steam releases exported from s&box: 'We signed the new license with Valve this week, allowing us to allow people to export games from s&box's editor and ship them as standalone games on Steam without paying us anything.'

Standalone export is still in PREVIEW and approval-gated. Docs (last updated ~26 Apr 2026) state distribution requires approval from Valve, that Facepunch is piloting with a few selected people first (My Summer Cottage as the first title), and instruct developers not to distribute exported builds without a license, directing them to standalone@facepunch.com. No evidence of general availability as of July 2026.

Garry Newman on the remaining work as of the license announcement: 'We still have work to do on our end. We need to create a license between Facepunch and the people shipping games, then double and triple check everything is legit.'
Standalone s&box games may be published to other storefronts only if the game is also on Steam — an itch.io-only or web-only release is not permitted under the license.

facts.claim: s&box supports PC export only. There is no console, mobile, or browser/WebAssembly export target.

Platform (non-standalone) games are restricted by a code accesslist: after compilation the assembly is scanned and refuses to load if it touches disallowed types. System.IO.File and variants, Process.Start, DllImport, and reflection are blocked; a virtual BaseFileSystem is provided instead.
Standalone builds can disable the whitelist entirely for full .NET runtime access, but doing so makes the game unpublishable to the s&box platform.

s&box uses C# on .NET 10. Gameplay code lives as ordinary .cs files in a `code/` folder at project root, tracked and hot-reloaded automatically; the project uses a modern .slnx solution openable from VS 2022/2026, VS Code, Cursor, or Rider. Saving a .cs or .razor file recompiles and applies the change while still in Play mode.

2D is natively supported: a Sprite resource and SpriteRenderer component now exist in-engine (Facepunch's separate sbox-spritetools library is explicitly marked OBSOLETE as a result), CameraComponent exposes orthographic projection with an OrthographicSize parameter, pixelated texture filtering is available, and a tileset editor shipped around the July 2026 update.

A top-down 2D Vampire-Survivors-like roguelite already exists on s&box. It was originally built on the legacy Entity system and later had to be re-created using the 2D Sprite Tools — a concrete instance of the breaking-change rewrite tax on this exact genre.

Facepunch's own documentation warned during the preview period that 'the C# API and tools are in a preview stage of development, with breaking changes happening often and the API not yet complete.'

System requirements — Minimum: Windows 10 64-bit, Core i5-7500 / Ryzen 5 1600, 8 GB RAM, GTX 1050 or RX 470/570 (4 GB). Recommended: Windows 11 64-bit, i7-9700K / Ryzen 7 3700, 16 GB RAM, GTX 1070 / RX 580. Intel integrated graphics are explicitly NOT supported; AMD APUs work.

s&box EULA: users 'own all rights in any original games and experiences you make using the s&box engine' (excluding Facepunch Property), but grant Facepunch 'a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free, sub-licensable, assignable licence over your Experiences.' Users must not 'infringe any third party rights.' Facepunch: 'If you break the rules in this EULA... we may temporarily or permanently suspend or cancel your access to s&box without prior warning' and remove Experiences, with no refunds.

Play Fund terms: creators 'do not have any right to compensation in relation to their experiences or use of s&box'; Facepunch 'operates The Play Fund at its sole and absolute discretion' and may suspend or discontinue it at any time. There is no direct game-sales channel for creators on the platform itself.

s&box monetization rules prohibit monetizing packages that use copyrighted material or that repackage someone else's work without real creativity; permitted sources are sbox.game content (implicit author permission), your own content, or openly licensed material.
Facepunch operates a public DMCA takedown reporting system for s&box packages, and publishes the claimant's full legal name, address, and contact details on the resulting takedown notice page.

AI coding agents currently struggle with s&box for four structural reasons: training data predates the Nov 2025 open-source release; 's&box C# isn't Unity C#... The component lifecycle, the networking model, the scene system... none of it maps'; 's&box runs a restricted .NET subset' so agents emit blocked APIs; and 'the total volume of s&box-specific code and documentation available on the open internet is a fraction of what exists for established engines.' ActionGraph visual scripting 'can't be automated' by text-based agents. Published 28 March 2026.

Headless execution exists via dedicated servers, which run without rendering by design. The configuration surface is deliberately tiny — five command-line switches (+game, +hostname, +net_game_server_token, +port, +net_query_port), one JSON file, and two branch options. Launch is package-oriented (+game <packageIdent>), not script-oriented.
The s&box editor is Windows-only, and s&box ships for Windows only.

entityPerfNotes:
Yes, technically — but only if you refuse to use the engine's main abstraction, which erases most of the reason to pick it.

The naive approach (2,000 GameObjects each carrying a SpriteRenderer) is the wrong one. Source 2's scene graph is tuned for hundreds of comparatively expensive objects — meshes with materials, physics bodies, culling volumes — not thousands of trivial textured quads. Per-GameObject cost is transform hierarchy maintenance, component update dispatch, per-object culling, and draw submission. Facepunch has been actively optimizing here (prefab/GameObject cloning is now ~2x faster, rendering work has yielded "40-50+ FPS" jumps), which tells you the baseline overhead was significant enough to be worth chasing. Spawning and despawning 2,000 pooled GameObjects per frame-ish is exactly the pattern that hurts, and it also fights the spec's "zero allocation in the hot loop" rule, since GameObject/Component churn allocates on the managed heap in ways you do not fully control.

The approach that actually works is the one this spec is already architected for, and it is a point in C#'s favor. Keep the simulation in flat, pre-allocated arrays — ideally arrays of structs for position/velocity/HP/flags — drive it from a single fixed-60Hz accumulator, run the spatial hash over indices rather than objects, and never touch the scene graph in the simulation at all. Then render the whole entity set as one batched/instanced pass: a custom render object (SceneCustomObject / the Graphics + RenderAttributes path) that writes interpolated quads into a vertex buffer once per frame under an orthographic CameraComponent. Source 2 will draw 2,000 instanced quads without noticing; on the GPU side this is a rounding error. C# helps you here more than JS did: real value types, contiguous memory, Span<T>, no boxing, and a GC you can keep entirely quiet with pooling and struct arrays. The 60Hz sim with interpolated rendering, the pooling discipline, and the 64px spatial hash all port cleanly and would likely run FASTER than the Canvas 2D original, where per-entity ctx draw calls are the real bottleneck.

Three caveats that matter more than the raw ceiling:

1. That custom-rendering path is the least-documented corner of s&box and has almost no public code corpus. An AI agent will not find it reliably, and will default to the GameObject-per-entity pattern that does not scale. You would be hand-holding the agent through the single hardest, least-exampled part of the engine — inverting the project's core delivery assumption.

2. The emoji placeholder strategy breaks. In Canvas 2D, `ctx.fillText('🦈', x, y)` is a one-liner and the entire art pipeline is free until you want real art. There is no equivalent world-space emoji draw in a Source 2 scene. Razor/UI text is screen-space and would collapse at 2,000 instances. You would have to pre-bake an emoji glyph atlas to a texture before M1 — meaning the spec's "do not block on art" de-risking pillar, which is what makes a solo dev able to reach a fun-check at milestone M1, has to be re-engineered before you can even start. Ironically the SpriteAtlas module the spec defers to "later" becomes mandatory work on day one.

3. Baseline engine cost eats your headroom on the target hardware. The Canvas 2D build's floor is a browser tab. The s&box build's floor is a full Source 2 runtime — 8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB recommended, and Intel integrated graphics flatly unsupported. "2,000 entities at 60 FPS on a mid-range laptop" is not just about your entity loop; on a very common class of mid-range laptop the game will not launch at all.
publishingPaths:
There are exactly two, and both are worse than what the developer already has.

PATH A — publish on the s&box platform. Available today, no approval needed, and this is what "easy publishing" presumably meant. The problem is the destination. The entire platform has ~695 concurrent players as of 25 July 2026, down from a 6,762 peak on release day (28 Apr 2026); June averaged 748 versus April's 4,106, a 59.5% one-month collapse and ~90% off peak. Every one of those players paid $19.99 to be there. Your game competes for that pool against every other package on the platform, on a front page that launched so saturated with AI-generated content that Steam reviews landed at "Mixed" (~44%) and Garry Newman publicly committed to pushing "obviously AI-created slop off the main page." A solo, AI-agent-built game whose shipping art direction is emoji and procedurally drawn shapes will be pattern-matched as exactly that. And there is no way to sell it: the platform has no direct creator sales channel, only The Play Fund — which the EULA states creators have "no right to compensation" from, which Facepunch "operates at its sole and absolute discretion," and which it may "suspend or discontinue at any time." It was doubled to $1M after launch backlash, spread across every creator on the platform. You would also be inside the code whitelist here — no System.IO, no reflection — which constrains the offline harness.

PATH B — export standalone and sell on Steam. This is the path with real commercial upside, and it is not open. Facepunch signed the enabling Valve license in late March 2026 and the terms are genuinely good (zero royalties, zero revenue share, full .NET with the whitelist off). But as of the latest documentation (updated ~26 Apr 2026, with no evidence of change through July 2026) it remains in preview: distribution requires approval from Valve, Facepunch is piloting with a small set of hand-picked developers (My Summer Cottage first), and the docs instruct you not to distribute exported builds without a license, pointing you at standalone@facepunch.com. Garry's own words on what remains: "We still have work to do on our end. We need to create a license between Facepunch and the people shipping games, then double and triple check everything is legit." For a game whose 19 characters are 1:1 mapped onto Gawr Gura, Goku, Naruto, Sasuke, and Light Yagami, that "double and triple check everything is legit" review is not a formality — it is the exact review most likely to stall or reject this specific project. And once through, you still face full Steam Direct: $100 fee, review, and a saturated Vampire-Survivors-like genre.

WHAT YOU CANNOT DO AT ALL:
- itch.io as a standalone or primary release. The standalone license reportedly permits other storefronts only if the game is also on Steam, so the fastest and cheapest indie path is contractually closed.
- Browser/HTML5 anywhere. No WebAssembly target. That means no playable-in-browser itch page, no Newgrounds, no Poki, no embeddable free demo — and the browser demo is the single most effective audience-building tool available to a solo dev in this genre.
- Consoles. No PlayStation, Xbox, or Switch export.
- Mobile. No iOS or Android, which also kills the spec's touch-control requirement.
- Mac, Linux, or Steam Deck. Windows only, for both the editor and the player.

For contrast, the spec as written ships TODAY: upload the folder to itch.io, it plays in the browser for free with no install and no paywall, and it simultaneously works as a downloadable, on any OS, on any laptop including Intel iGPU machines and Chromebooks. Choosing s&box means trading a live, zero-friction, multi-channel distribution position for a queue.
portCostFromSpec:
Effectively a total rewrite — call it 90-100% of the written spec, with the highest-risk parts rewritten first and the project's core de-risking strategy invalidated at the start.

The spec is not merely web-adjacent, it is web-native by mandate. Section 1 requires "HTML5 + Canvas 2D. Vanilla JavaScript (ES modules). No build step required — it must run by opening index.html," plus "zero external runtime dependencies," offline playability, localStorage persistence, WebAudio synthesis, the Gamepad API, and touch controls. Section 17 then re-encodes these as pass/fail acceptance criteria. There is no incremental migration; JavaScript does not run in s&box.

WHAT SURVIVES AS DESIGN (the genuinely valuable part, ~all of it):
Everything from Section 2 onward — the 19 characters and their 4 ability pillars, 24 relics, 22 upgrades with 8 levels each, 8 evolutions, 7 stages with hazards and modifiers, ~23 enemy types, 8 elite affixes, 7 bosses with telegraphs and phases, the 4 gacha banners with soft/hard pity and 50/50 rules, the shrine, bonds, achievements, and codex. This is the majority of the document's page count and it is engine-agnostic. The `/src/data` "all content is plain data objects, adding a character edits exactly ONE file" architecture also survives conceptually — it becomes static C# classes or JSON resources.

WHAT SURVIVES AS ARCHITECTURE:
The 60Hz accumulator with decoupled interpolated rendering, object pooling with zero hot-loop allocation, the 64px spatial hash broadphase, XP gem merging above 400, off-screen culling and enemy teleporting, the 60-damage-number cap with aggregation, the 800-particle cap, the single `damage.js` choke point, and the two-stream seedable RNG (mulberry32/xorshift128 port trivially to C#) — all of these are correct engineering that transfers directly, and several get BETTER in C#.

WHAT MUST BE REWRITTEN LINE BY LINE (~30 modules):
Every file in /src/core, /src/render, /src/game, /src/data, /src/ui, /src/scenes. JS to C#, with different idioms throughout.

WHAT MUST BE RE-ARCHITECTED, NOT JUST TRANSLATED:
- The entire render layer (renderer.js, camera.js, particles.js, damageNumbers.js, screenShake.js, spriteAtlas.js). This is the deepest and riskiest change: immediate-mode Canvas draw calls become either a retained scene graph or, correctly, a custom instanced-quad render object. Different paradigm, not a port.
- The placeholder art strategy — and this is the one that actually hurts. The spec's `{ shape, color, outline, size, emoji }` visual object with emoji + procedural shapes is what lets a solo dev reach the M1 "is this ALREADY satisfying?" gate without any art. There is no world-space emoji draw in Source 2. You must build and bake an emoji glyph atlas before M0/M1 can produce anything. The SpriteAtlas module the spec explicitly defers becomes mandatory day-one infrastructure, and "Do NOT block on art" is broken by the engine choice.
- The headless harness. `?sim=1&char=rin&stage=2&seed=42` becomes a command-line or console-command entry point. Feasible — dedicated servers are genuinely headless — but s&box's launch model is package-oriented with a deliberately tiny five-switch surface, and 100x-speed decoupled-from-render stepping in a Source 2 host is meaningfully more awkward than `node sim.js`. If you stay on-platform, the whitelist also blocks System.IO, so writing CSV sweep results across 19 characters x 7 stages must route through BaseFileSystem.
- Audio: WebAudio synthesized SFX (square/saw blips, noise bursts, rising arpeggios) becomes s&box's audio system. Runtime synthesis is not the native idiom; expect to pre-render or re-approach.
- UI: hud/menus/levelUp/gacha/results/roster/shrine move to Razor components — a different model from Canvas-drawn UI, though Razor is decent.
- Persistence: localStorage JSON blob to s&box's BaseFileSystem/FileSystem.Data. The `schemaVersion` field and migration stub port cleanly. Genuinely low-cost.

WHAT IS SIMPLY DELETED:
Touch input and the virtual-stick layout (no mobile target). Browser-restart save testing. "No build step" (you now need Windows + the s&box editor + asset compilation). "No network requests / offline-playable" (becomes a dependency on a $20 platform, or on an approval-gated export).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA THAT BECOME UNACHIEVABLE:
"Opens from index.html with no build step and no network requests" (impossible), "Save/load survives a browser restart" (N/A), "Keyboard, mouse, gamepad, and touch all fully playable" (touch impossible), and "60 FPS with 2,000 entities on a mid-range laptop" is now conditional — Intel iGPU laptops cannot run it at all.

Bottom line on cost: the design document remains ~90% valuable and the M2-M7 content work is largely unchanged in effort. But M0, M1, and M8 are rebuilt from zero against a sparsely documented API, in a language the spec was not written in, using the engine's least-exampled rendering path, with an AI agent operating well outside its strongest domain — and the M1 fun-gate is delayed by mandatory atlas work that the original spec deliberately deferred. If the goal is to ship this game, keep the stack the spec already specifies, ship free on itch.io in-browser to build an audience, and reserve a Steam build for a native wrapper later. If the developer wants C#-grade simulation performance and a real Steam path, MonoGame or Godot (C#) deliver every benefit s&box offers here — real 2D tooling, plain-text code, huge AI training corpus, mature 2D renderers — with none of the platform lock-in, none of the approval gating, no whitelist, no third-party takedown authority over an IP-parody game, and full web, mobile, console, Mac, Linux, and Steam Deck targets.
